analysis.one_liner: Gives workers easier union recognition, binding first contracts, tougher employer penalties, and public-sector bargaining rights.
analysis.headline: The Workplace Democracy Act, backed by 20 House members, never got a hearing or vote; it died in a House committee when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the country's main labor law to make it much easier for workers to form unions and much costlier for employers to fight them. Workers could unionize by collecting signed cards instead of winning a secret-ballot election; unions stuck without a first contract could force binding arbitration; employers who violate workers' rights would face mandatory reinstatement, fines of at least $10,000, government-contract bans, and triple-damage lawsuits. It would also create a national commission guaranteeing collective bargaining rights to state and local government employees, including most of those in states where they currently have none, and require employer-employee joint control of single-employer pension plans. The bill went to the House committee that handles labor law and never came out.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize unions, existing union members seeking stronger remedies against illegal employer conduct, and millions of state and local government employees — teachers, nurses, sanitation workers — in states that currently give them little or no bargaining rights.

how_it_helps.text: Workers could win union recognition when a majority of employees in a bargaining unit sign union cards, removing the secret-ballot election stage that employers can use to campaign against the union and delay recognition [S2][S3].

If no collective bargaining agreement is reached within 45 days of certification, the union could send the dispute to compulsory, binding arbitration, ending the practice of employers refusing to sign a first contract [S2][S3].
The bill repeals prohibitions on certain strikes, secondary boycotts, and hot cargo agreements, restoring forms of economic pressure that federal law has banned since 1947 [S2][S3].

Employers found to have willfully violated the law would face mandatory reinstatement of fired workers while the case is pending, civil penalties of at least $10,000 per violation, required NLRB injunctions, debarment from federal contracts for up to three years, and treble-damage suits for workers illegally fired or discriminated against [S2][S3].

It repeals the provision that lets states ban union-security agreements, so workers in right-to-work states could negotiate contracts requiring everyone who benefits from the contract to pay dues-equivalent fees [S2][S3].

A new National Public Employment Relations Commission would guarantee state and local government employees the right to organize, bargain, and, except for firefighters and public safety officers, strike — rights roughly half the states currently deny or sharply limit (general knowledge; the commission and its powers are in the bill text) [S2][S3].

The National Labor Relations Act would apply to U.S. companies and their subsidiaries operating in countries with a U.S. free trade agreement, letting those workers file unfair-labor-practice complaints against the U.S. parent company [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially those with anti-union practices — would face higher penalties, binding arbitration, boycotts by other unions' workers, and card-check organizing; state and local governments would become employers under a federal bargaining regime with new costs; and neutral businesses caught in legalized secondary boycotts would bear pressure aimed at others.

drawbacks.text: Card-check recognition ends the secret-ballot election as the standard route to union certification, meaning a union could be certified as the exclusive representative of all workers in a unit based on signed cards without those workers ever voting on it [S2][S3].

Compulsory binding arbitration of first contracts means a third party could impose wage and work-rule terms on both sides, and for state and local governments, awards can bind even the appropriating legislative body [S3].

Repealing the secondary-boycott and hot-cargo prohibitions would allow unions to pressure neutral companies to stop doing business with a targeted employer, drawing businesses that are not party to any labor dispute into the fight [S2][S3].

Guaranteeing public employees the right to strike would give public-sector unions leverage against their own government employers, raising the risk of service interruptions in schools, hospitals, and other government functions [S3].

The bill preempts state labor laws where they are less protective and creates a new five-member federal commission with subpoena power, adding a new federal enforcement apparatus over state and local employers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill reverses most of the legal changes since 1947 that tilted organizing and bargaining toward employers, and it does so at genuine cost: employers would face real financial exposure, governments would lose flexibility as employers, and some private parties would lose immunity from secondary pressure. The card-check and mandatory-arbitration provisions are the most contested — supporters see them as the only way to make organizing work when employers can drag out elections and refuse contracts; critics see them as removing workers' final say and locking in contracts no one voted on. It is a broad, one-sided transfer of workplace power toward unions, by design.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee, then to its Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernard Sanders introduced the bill on March 29, 1995 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities and, two weeks later, to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].
The bill drew 19 cosponsors, all Democrats, in a House where Republicans had won control of every standing committee in the 1994 elections [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced card-check organizing, binding arbitration, boycotts, and much higher penalties, and state and local governments that would have been brought under a federal bargaining regime, are better off because the bill died; current labor law stayed as it was.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was an independent allied with Democrats and all 19 cosponsors were Democrats; with Republicans controlling the House and its committees after 1994, the bill never moved, and no roll-call vote was ever taken.

industries.note: Card-check recognition, mandatory first-contract arbitration, legalized secondary boycotts, minimum $10,000 penalties per willful violation, contract debarment, and treble-damage exposure would have sharply raised the cost of resisting unions. Their gain from the bill's death is the status quo remaining unchanged.

industries.industry: State and local governments as employers
industries.note: The bill would have federalized public-sector bargaining, required union-security payments, and subjected governments to binding impasse arbitration, with costs falling on budgets. As the employers covered by Title II, their interest ran against the workers the bill aimed to protect.
Unions would gain the recognition route, enforcement teeth, and strike rights that make organizing and bargaining effective; the bill's core purpose is to restore union bargaining power to workers.

Title III would require joint trusteeship of single-employer pension plans, giving participants equal representation with employers over plan assets — a loss of sole control for sponsoring employers and a gain in fiduciary oversight for savers.
